meta.title: Who really said "A room without books is like a body without a soul"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Cicero. The sentence is Sir John Lubbock’s, from The Pleasures of Life (1887) — his own paraphrase of a very different remark Cicero made to Atticus.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A room without books is like a body without a soul'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Cicero — Sir John Lubbock wrote it in 1887, paraphrasing Cicero. Quote Investigator finds no Ciceronian original.

answer.label: Not Cicero — actually Sir John Lubbock
answer.authorDates: 1834–1913 · English banker, politician, naturalist & popular essayist
answer.sourceLine: The sentence in circulation is Lubbock’s own. In the lecture “A Song of Books,” collected in The Pleasures of Life, Part I (first printed June 1887), he wrote: “Cicero described a room without books, as a body without a soul.” That is Lubbock characterising Cicero, not quoting him. What Cicero actually wrote — to Atticus, in Ad Atticum 4.8 — is that once his librarian Tyrannio had arranged his books, his house seemed to have acquired a soul. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no evidence Cicero ever framed the thought as this aphorism.

source.excerpt: Cicero described a room without books, as a body without a soul. But it is by no means necessary to be a philosopher to love reading.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ examined the adage in 2023 and concluded it has “found no evidence that Cicero crafted this adage,” hypothesising instead that it grew out of Cicero’s letter to Atticus.
We read Lubbock’s book ourselves: the sentence “Cicero described a room without books, as a body without a soul” appears on p. 61 of The Pleasures of Life, Part I ↗, in the chapter “A Song of Books.”

Cicero’s actual line is in Ad Atticum 4.8. E. O. Winstedt’s Loeb translation renders it “Since Tyrannio has arranged my books, the house seems to have acquired a soul” — Cicero: Letters to Atticus I (1912) ↗. A house acquiring a soul when its books are shelved is not the same claim as a bookless room lacking one.
Wikiquote files the line under “Disputed” on its Cicero page ↗ and points to the same Lubbock source.
source.excerptNote: Lubbock’s own words, p. 61 of the Macmillan printing linked below. The clause is a description of Cicero; the quotation marks the internet later added around it are what turned it into a Cicero quote.

author.name: Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury)
author.heading: About Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury)
author.metaLine: 1834–1913 · English banker, Liberal MP, naturalist & essayist
author.bio: Sir John Lubbock, 1st Baron Avebury, was a banker and Liberal MP who was also a working naturalist — a neighbour and protégé of Darwin, and the man who gave English the terms Palaeolithic and Neolithic. In Parliament he carried the Bank Holidays Act 1871, which is why bank holidays were once nicknamed “St Lubbock’s Days.” The Pleasures of Life (1887), the source of this sentence, was a runaway popular success that went through printing after printing.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A description of Cicero became a quotation from Cicero, and then drifted further.

items.why: Cicero’s genuine remark (Ad Atticum 4.8) is about his own house gaining a soul once his books were arranged. QI ↗ found no Ciceronian text containing the aphorism itself.

His 1887 sentence “Cicero described a room without books, as a body without a soul” is the earliest appearance of this exact room without books phrasing that we or QI ↗ could locate. He wrote it as a description of Cicero, not as a quotation from him.
QI ↗ records the Chesterton credit appearing by 2005 and calls it unsupported, noting that “Chesterton” and “Cicero” sit close together in alphabetised quotation lists.
QI ↗ gives the earliest appearance of the adage attributed to Cicero as Yates’s 1844 A Winter in Italy — but in the form “a house without a library,” not “a room without books.”

misattribution.truthLine: Cicero said something adjacent and better: that his house acquired a soul once his books were finally shelved. The aphorism people quote is Lubbock’s summary of him ↗, written eighteen centuries later.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lubbock was not trying to put words in Cicero’s mouth. “A Song of Books” was a lecture for the Working Men’s College, and its whole argument is that reading is a pleasure available to anyone — “it is by no means necessary to be a philosopher to love reading,” as the very next sentence says. Invoking Cicero was a rhetorical warrant, not a citation.
detailsBody: Lubbock is a repeat offender, though not a dishonest one. The Pleasures of Life is also the earliest documented source for “Music is a moral law…” — a passage universally credited to Plato that appears in no Platonic text. Both lines entered circulation the same way: Lubbock wrote an elegant summary of an ancient author, and later readers mistook the summary for the original.

The drift is easy to trace in the reference books. Burton Stevenson’s Home Book of Quotations (1949) printed the line under CICERO while honestly citing Lubbock in the parenthesis; the Concise Columbia Dictionary of Quotations (1989) went the other way and credited Lubbock outright. Between the two sits the modern internet, which kept the Cicero name and dropped the parenthesis. Both datapoints are documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
context.pull: A description of Cicero, quoted for a century as Cicero.
